lead: This unit is about limits of lists and limits of sums. You learn when a sequence settles on a number, when an infinite series adds up to a finite value, and how to prove both with tests. After it you can classify series as convergent, divergent, absolute or conditional, and find where a power series converges.
about: The unit starts with sequences in 3.1: a sequence is a function on natural numbers, and convergence is an ε-N statement. Chapter 3.2 turns a sequence into a series by partial sums. Chapter 3.3 gives comparison, integral, ratio and root tests for positive series; only a few universities teach this full set at this depth. Chapter 3.4 handles alternating signs with the Leibnitz test, and 3.5 separates absolute from conditional convergence. Chapter 3.6 moves to power series and the radius of convergence. Chapter 3.7 adds Raabe's and the logarithmic test for the ratio-test case that gives 1; only a few universities teach these. Chapter 3.8 closes with Cauchy sequences and completeness, the property that makes limits exist in the real numbers.

chapters.idea: A sequence is a list a₁, a₂, a₃, … of real numbers, and it converges to L when its terms eventually stay inside every chosen band around L.
chapters.depth: Definition of a sequence as a function a: ℕ → ℝ from natural numbers to real numbers; notation aₙ. ε-N definition of limit: for every positive real ε there is an integer N such that |aₙ−L|<ε for all n≥N. Bounded, monotone and eventually monotone sequences; algebra of limits; uniqueness of limit; subsequences; limsup and liminf as largest and smallest subsequential limits; Archimedean property used to choose N. Some syllabi call this 'convergence of sequences' or 'limit of a sequence'.

figure.aria: The points of the sequence enter the band between 2.99 and 3.01 and stay there after n passes 499, showing convergence to 3 for ε = 0.01.

chapters.example: Show from the ε-N definition that lim (3n+1)/(n+2) = 3. For ε = 0.01, find an N that works. Solution: |(3n+1)/(n+2) − 3| = 5/(n+2). Need 5/(n+2) < 0.01, so n+2 > 500, n > 498. Take N = 499.
chapters.trap: Replacing 'for all n ≥ N' by 'for infinitely many n', or assuming a bounded sequence must converge. A sequence can oscillate between 0 and 1 and stay bounded.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 ideas of a function and inequalities; absolute value.
chapters.leave: Limit superior and inferior proofs and Cauchy completeness go to 3.8; series start in 3.2.

chapters.idea: An infinite series is the limit of its partial sums, so its convergence is exactly the convergence of a sequence.
chapters.depth: Definition Σaₙ = lim S_N where S_N = a₁+…+a_N. Geometric series and its sum a/(1−r) for |r|<1; telescoping series; nth term test (if aₙ does not tend to 0 the series diverges); algebra of convergent series; Cauchy criterion for series; harmonic series divergence by grouping or integral comparison. Some syllabi say 'series of real numbers' or 'partial sums'.

figure.aria: The flow shows terms forming partial sums, and the series converges only when those partial sums have a limit.

chapters.example: Find Σ_{n=1}∞ 1/(n(n+1)) using partial fractions. Solution: 1/(n(n+1)) = 1/n − 1/(n+1). Then S_N = 1 − 1/(N+1), so the limit is 1.
chapters.trap: Thinking aₙ→0 proves convergence. The harmonic series has aₙ→0 but diverges.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for the definition of a limit of a sequence.
chapters.leave: Tests for convergence are in 3.3; alternating signs in 3.4; power series in 3.6.

chapters.idea: Comparison, integral, ratio and root tests decide convergence by comparing a series with a known series, an integral, or a limit of ratios.
chapters.depth: Positive-term series only. Direct comparison and limit comparison with p-series Σ1/nᵖ, which converges iff p>1. Integral test with f positive, continuous, decreasing and f(n)=aₙ; convergence of Σaₙ and ∫₁∞ f(x)dx are equivalent. Ratio test: L = lim |a_{n+1}/aₙ|; converges if L<1, diverges if L>1, no conclusion if L=1. Root test: L = lim |aₙ|^{1/n}; same rules. Cauchy condensation as a one-line variant. Some syllabi say 'D'Alembert's ratio test' and 'Cauchy's root test'. Only a few universities teach all four in one unit.

figure.aria: A decision tree sends a positive series to the ratio test for factorials, the root test for nth powers, comparison for p-series shapes, and the integral test when an antiderivative is easy.

chapters.example: Test Σ_{n=1}∞ n²/2ⁿ. Ratio: |a_{n+1}/aₙ| = ((n+1)²/2^{n+1})/(n²/2ⁿ) = (1+1/n)²/2 → 1/2 < 1, so the series converges.
chapters.trap: Using the ratio or root test when L = 1 and calling the series convergent. The test gives no answer; switch to comparison or Raabe.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 and 3.2; Unit 1 limits; Unit 2 improper integrals for the integral test.
chapters.leave: Alternating signs to 3.4; Raabe and logarithmic refinements to 3.7; power series to 3.6.

chapters.idea: In an alternating series the signs flip, and if the sizes decrease steadily to zero the partial sums close in on a limit.
chapters.depth: Definition Σ(−1)^{n+1}bₙ with bₙ>0. Leibnitz test: if bₙ decreases and bₙ→0, the series converges; remainder estimate |S − S_N| ≤ b_{N+1}. Alternating harmonic series. Some syllabi spell 'Leibniz'. Do not discuss absolute convergence here beyond one pointer.

figure.aria: Partial sums of the alternating harmonic series jump above and below the line ln 2 ≈ 0.693 and move closer to it.

chapters.example: Test Σ_{n=1}∞ (−1)^{n+1} n/(n²+1). Here bₙ = n/(n²+1). bₙ→0 and bₙ decreases for n≥1 because its derivative (1−n²)/(n²+1)² is ≤0. By the Leibnitz test the series converges.
chapters.trap: Checking only bₙ→0 and not that bₙ is decreasing. An alternating series with terms not decreasing can still diverge or need another test.
chapters.prereq: 3.2 for series and partial sums; 3.1 for limits.
chapters.leave: Absolute convergence and rearrangement go to 3.5; comparison tests to 3.3.

chapters.idea: Absolute convergence means Σ|aₙ| converges; it is stronger than ordinary convergence, while conditional convergence means the series converges but not absolutely.
chapters.depth: Definitions; theorem absolute convergence ⇒ convergence; converse false (alternating harmonic). Conditional series can be rearranged to change the sum (Riemann rearrangement theorem, statement only). Tests: use 3.3 on Σ|aₙ| first; if it diverges, test the original with 3.4. Some syllabi say 'convergence with absolute values'.

figure.aria: Nested sets place absolutely convergent series inside all convergent series, with the alternating harmonic series in the outer ring.

chapters.example: Classify Σ_{n=1}∞ (−1)ⁿ/√(n+1). Absolute test: Σ1/√(n+1) diverges because p=1/2. Original series: bₙ=1/√(n+1) decreases to 0, so it converges by Leibnitz. Hence it is conditionally convergent.
chapters.trap: Treating absolute convergence and convergence as the same. Every absolutely convergent series converges, but the alternating harmonic series converges and Σ1/n diverges.
chapters.prereq: 3.2 for series; 3.3 for absolute tests; 3.4 for alternating series.
chapters.leave: Rearrangement proofs and power series convergence go to later chapters; only the statement of rearrangement belongs here.

chapters.idea: A power series is an infinite polynomial Σcₙ(x−a)ⁿ; it converges inside a symmetric interval around a whose size is the radius of convergence R.
chapters.depth: Definition with centre a and coefficients cₙ. Radius from the ratio test on cₙ: R = lim |cₙ/c_{n+1}| when the limit exists, or R = 1/limsup |cₙ|^{1/n}. Convergence for |x−a|<R, divergence for |x−a|>R; endpoints x=a±R checked separately. Interval of convergence notation. Term-by-term differentiation and integration inside R stated, with a pointer to Unit 1 Taylor series. Some syllabi say 'power series in x'.

nodes.label: Check x = a−R and x = a+R

figure.aria: The flow finds R from coefficients, marks the open interval of convergence, and then tests the two endpoints separately.

chapters.example: Find the radius and interval of convergence of Σ_{n=1}∞ xⁿ/n. Ratio: |a_{n+1}/aₙ| = |x| n/(n+1) → |x|, so R=1. At x=1, Σ1/n diverges. At x=−1, Σ(−1)ⁿ/n converges by Leibnitz. Interval: [−1,1).
chapters.trap: Stopping at R = 1 and writing (−1,1). The two endpoints need separate tests and may behave differently.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 and 3.2; 3.3 for ratio and root tests; 3.4 for endpoint checks.
chapters.leave: Taylor series and differentiation of power series belong to Unit 1; complex power series are outside this unit.

chapters.idea: When the ratio test gives 1, Raabe's test measures how far the ratio is from 1 and compares it with 1 + p/n; the logarithmic test does the same comparison on a log scale.
chapters.depth: Positive-term series. Raabe: if n(aₙ/a_{n+1} − 1) → L, then Σaₙ converges for L>1, diverges for L<1, no conclusion for L=1. Logarithmic test: if log(1/aₙ)/log n → L, then convergence behaves like Σ1/n^L: converges for L>1, diverges for L<1. State only as a refinement after 3.3. Only a few universities teach these.

figure.aria: The Raabe expression n(aₙ/aₙ₊₁ − 1) rises toward 1/2, which is below 1 and predicts divergence.

chapters.example: Test Σ_{n=1}∞ (1·3·5···(2n−1))/(2·4·6···2n). Let aₙ be the nth term. Then a_{n+1}/aₙ = (2n+1)/(2n+2), so aₙ/a_{n+1} = (2n+2)/(2n+1). Thus n(aₙ/a_{n+1} − 1) = n/(2n+1) → 1/2 < 1, so the series diverges.
chapters.trap: Writing the ratio upside down. Raabe uses aₙ/a_{n+1}, not a_{n+1}/aₙ; reversing it turns a divergent series into a false convergent one.
chapters.leave: Absolute convergence to 3.5; power series to 3.6; completeness to 3.8.

chapters.idea: A Cauchy sequence has terms that get close to each other; the real line is complete because every such sequence has a real limit, while the rationals have gaps.
chapters.depth: Definition: for every positive real ε there is N with |a_m−a_n|<ε for all m,n≥N. Every convergent sequence is Cauchy; in ℝ every Cauchy sequence converges (completeness). Cauchy criterion for series: Σaₙ converges iff its partial sums are Cauchy. Completeness property: every nonempty set bounded above has a least upper bound; Archimedean property. Contrast ℚ: decimal truncations of √2 are Cauchy in ℚ but have no rational limit. Only a few universities teach this.

figure.aria: The flow shows a Cauchy sequence getting a real limit because of completeness, with a dashed branch showing the rational gap at √2.

chapters.example: Show aₙ = 1/n is Cauchy. For ε = 0.01, find N. Solution: for m,n ≥ N, |1/m − 1/n| ≤ 1/m + 1/n ≤ 2/N. Need 2/N < 0.01, so N > 200. Take N = 201. The definition needs no limit; in ℝ the sequence converges to 0.
chapters.trap: Saying every Cauchy sequence converges in every ordered field. It fails in ℚ; completeness is a property of ℝ, not of the definition alone.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 and 3.2; absolute value and inequalities; supremum idea.
chapters.leave: Construction of ℝ from Dedekind cuts or Cauchy sequences is beyond this unit; series tests stay in 3.3–3.7.
